claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by gas-environment-induced selective oxidation.
Selective oxidation produces a non-uniform mixed Al–Ti-rich oxide scale.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Ti oxidize rapidly.
Oxidizing conditions produce a thick, poorly adherent oxide scale.
The thick, poorly adherent scale generates interfacial stresses and microcracking.
Under reducing conditions, limited oxygen availability causes incomplete oxidation and compositional gradients at the scale/alloy interface.
Compositional gradients under reducing conditions generate localized interfacial stresses.
The proposed surface degradation occurs without extensive alteration of the fcc matrix.
Bulk strength and fatigue properties are preserved until surface-initiated damage becomes critical.
The as-manufactured alloy has a uniform fcc matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy contains fine AM-induced cellular features.
The as-manufactured alloy has excellent strength and fatigue performance.
At 800 °C for 100 hours, synthetic-air exposure will produce a thicker oxide scale than exposure to 5% H2–Ar.
The oxide formed in synthetic air will be less adherent and will promote earlier microcrack formation and property degradation than the reducing-atmosphere scale.
Exposure to 5% H2–Ar will produce a thinner but compositionally disordered oxide scale.
The reducing-atmosphere scale will generate localized stress concentrations, but possibly to a lesser degree than the oxidizing-atmosphere scale.
Selective-oxidation effects become significant near or above 800 °C after exposures longer than approximately 50 hours.
Scale thickening and spallation initiate microcracks that eventually impair fatigue performance.
